us-ca8-89-f4th-686.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-89-f4th-686.citation: Paul Essel v. Merrick Garland, 89 F.4th 686 (8th Cir. 2023)
us-ca8-89-f4th-686.summary: The court treated the approved I-130 petition filed by Essel’s citizen spouse under the family-based immigration provisions as permitting Essel to seek adjustment of status, but emphasized that approval alone did not confer immigration status or guarantee eligibility. Because a final removal order was already in place, Essel needed to obtain reopening of the proceedings before pursuing adjustment.
excerpts: A United States citizen may file an I-130 petition with Immigration Services to request permanent resident status for an alien relative or spouse. See 8 U.S.C. § 1154(a)(1)(A)(i); 8 C.F.R. § 204.2(a)(1) (“A United States citizen or alien admitted for lawful permanent residence may file a [visa] petition on behalf of a spouse.

Though this approval did not itself grant any immigration status to Essel or guarantee his eligibility for a visa, it would normally allow him to apply for an adjustment of status. See 8 U.S.C. § 1255(a); Tebyasa v. Holder, 593 F.3d 707, 709 (8th Cir. 2010).
Because the Board already issued a final order of removal, Essel needed to file a motion to reopen with the Board to change his immigration status. See Tebyasa, 593 F.3d at 709; 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 C.F.R. § 204.2(a)(1), specifically the provision allowing a United States citizen or lawful permanent resident to file a petition on behalf of a spouse. That operative language remains substantively identical in the current text; the only discrepancy is the excerpt’s editorial “[visa]” insertion, while the 2025 amendment does not appear to alter this provision.

us-ca8-566-f3d-758.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-566-f3d-758.summary: The court applied the statutory and regulatory scheme governing conditional permanent residence based on marriage to a U.S. citizen. It held that an alien seeking a waiver of the joint-filing requirement must first establish that the qualifying marriage was entered into in good faith; only then does the Attorney General have discretion to grant the waiver and remove the conditions.
excerpts: Permanent-resident status conferred on the basis of a marriage to a U.S. citizen is granted initially on a conditional basis. Id. § 1186a(a)(l). Within ninety days prior to the two-year anniversary of the grant of conditional permanent-resident status, an alien can apply to have the conditional basis removed. Id. § 1186a(e)(3), (d)(2); 8 C.F.R. § 216.4(a)(1).

In order to establish eligibility for this good-faith marriage waiver or “hardship waiver,” the alien must first show that he or she entered into a “qualifying marriage ... in good faith.” Id. Only after the alien has established this fact does the Attorney General possess the discretion to grant the waiver and remove the conditional basis of the permanent-resident status. Id. If the Government denies the waiver application, the alien is entitled to seek review of the denial before the IJ during the course of removal proceedings. 8 C.F.R. § 216.5(f).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(a)(1), (c)(3), (d)(2), and (e)(3)–(4)(B), concerning conditional residence and the 90-day period for seeking removal of conditions. The 2011 amendment to § 1186a(a)(1) merely renumbered cross-references from subsections (g) to (h) after adding a new subsection (g), without changing the provision’s substantive function; the later amendments did not alter the interpreted requirements.

Ibrahimi interpreted 8 C.F.R. § 216.4(a)(1), particularly the requirement to file Form I-751 during the 90-day period before the second anniversary of conditional residence and the availability of a waiver when a joint petition cannot be filed. The current text preserves that timing requirement and waiver function; the cited excerpt is paraphrased rather than verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.
